COMMONWEALTH OF MASSACHUSETTS
DEPARTMENT OF ENVIRONMENTAL QUALITY ENGINEERING
AIR QUALITY
The particulate emissions associated with urban building demolition differ significantly from the incinerator and other stack emissions that are more usually the subject of study. First, demolition generates particulates at ground level, primarily through mechanical impact and crushing. Thus particulates are released at a low level. Due to the turbulent conditions associated with the impact of rubble on the ground, the effective height of release will vary between 6 and 18 feet.
Second, the demolition environment is confined by the presence of many structures, 25 to 30 feet high, and less than 50 feet from one another. Observation of the demolition process indicates that both horizontal and vertical diffusion of particulates are impeded by the proximity of these structures to the demolition site. A sample calculation (Exhibit 1) indicates that over 90 percent of a dust plume would be at an elevation of less than 60 feet at a downwind location of 300 feet, with no obstructions. Thus, the zone of significant impact with respect to a potential source-receptor interaction is confined to an area immediately adjacent to a demolition site.
Finally, measurement of the particles and an analysis of the results indicate that the geometric mean diameter of demolition particles from a wood frame building is 18 microns, with a standard deviation of 2.09. This indicates that there are very few particles of 10 microns or smaller which could affect human health.
None of these conditions means that there is no air quality impact from the proposed activity. However, they do indicate that major environmental impact is confined to the immediate vicinity of the site. These three conditions, plus the lack of any published demolition emission factors, led to a sampling and analysis procedure which was intended to characterize the localized particulate impacts in terms of their quantity, soiling potential and potential health effects.
Adequacy of the Sampling Sites
Given the lack of any published demolition emission factors, the major purpose of the sampling was to obtain information that would be used to develop emission factors. Therefore, sampling procedures were used that would yield the greatest dust concentrations at the locations of the nearest receptors. The sample data are shown in Exhibit 2.
Hi-vol samplers with 4 inch diameter filters were used for sampling periods of 10 to 120 minutes at distances of 11 to 50 feet from the demolition activity. The samplers were oriented horizontally to the dust envelope produced by the demolition procedures, at an elevation of approximately 5 feet where the greatest dust concentrations were observed. The sampling time was controlled by the dust build-up on the filter. (See Exhibits 1 and 2.) The concentrations of particulates obtained at the sampling sites were used to calculate emission rates through the use of the basic gaussian diffusion model. (See Exhibit 3.)
